sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: Objectives Wildlife–vehicle collisions (WVCs) impose a large and poorly measured toll on United States highways, yet most state crash databases never record which crashes involved an animal, so agencies cannot say how many they miss. This paper asks whether the crash records agencies already hold can be used to identify WVCs at the record level and to estimate how many go uncoded. Methods We assembled 4.9 million crash records from Colorado, Utah, Iowa, and Illinois, spanning 2007 to 2026. Each state’s schema was passed through a label-leakage screen that removes any field encoding animal involvement, and separately harmonized to a shared vocabulary for cross-state analysis. Labeled wildlife vehicle crashes are treated as ground-truth, with which Calibrated gradient-boosted classifiers were trained per state and read with Shapley additive explanations. Prevalence was then estimated directly from classifier scores using Adjusted Classify-and-Count and Maximum-Likelihood Prevalence Estimation, validated in-domain, across states, and against injected reporting gaps. Findings Detection quality is governed by how completely a crash is recorded, not by how rare WVCs are: at equivalent prevalence near four percent, feature-rich Utah reaches an average precision of 0.88 against 0.64 for feature-poor Colorado, and Utah exceeds Iowa despite Iowa’s threefold higher prevalence. A within-state richness curve with bootstrap confidence intervals confirms the effect with prevalence held fixed. Models rank records almost perfectly everywhere, but their calibration does not transfer, and prevalence estimates recover the true rate to within 0.001 in-domain. Novelty This work reframes WVC surveillance from predicting where collisions cluster to detecting which records are collisions and estimating how many are missing, using only data agencies already collect. Practical Applications Agencies can retrospectively flag unlogged WVCs in legacy files, quantify their true collision burden for mitigation funding, and learn which crash-report fields most improve detection before revising a reporting manual. Keywords : wildlife–vehicle collisions, crash records, under-reporting, quantification learning, gradient boosting, data quality

sections.heading: 1 INTRODUCTION
sections.text: Collisions between vehicles and large wild animals are among the most common crash types on rural highways yet among the least visible in the data that transportation agencies use to set priorities ( Bell et al., 2024 ; Jørgensen et al., 2025 ) . Wildlife-Vehicle Crashes (WVC) cost the United States above eight billion dollars, alongside tens of thousands of injuries and close to two hundred deaths ( Bell et al., 2024 ) . Earlier national accounting put large-mammal collisions at one to two million per year ( Huijser et al., 2009 ) . Texas alone recorded 51,522 animal-related crashes between 2010 and 2016, costing motorists roughly $1.3 billion annually ( Wilkins et al., 2019 ) . These figures share a fundamental limitation. Every one of them is built from crashes that were reported, coded, and retained, and the literature is unanimous that this is a fraction of what occurs. Maintenance crews recover five to ten carcasses for every collision that reaches a police report ( Wilkins et al., 2019 ) , and Montana’s transportation department counted 60,858 carcasses over a decade against 23,718 collisions logged by highway patrol over the same period ( Bell et al., 2024 ) . Despite the significant disparities, there has been no unified method to estimate the cost of unreported WVCs. This needed capability to address this gap is hinged on state crash reporting rules, which establishes what is recorded into crash report, and how. When North Dakota narrowed its reporting requirement to injury and fatality crashes in 2013, annual reported WVCs fell from 3,488 to 133, and seasonal effects that had been statistically detectable before the change became invisible afterwards purely through loss of sample size ( Jørgensen et al., 2025 ) . The same administrative dynamics that decides whether a crash is recorded also decides how richly it is described, and both decisions propagate into every downstream analysis an agency performs. Machine learning (ML) has been applied to this problem from a different perspective. A decade of work has treated WVCs as a spatial phenomenon and asked where collisions concentrate, fitting risk surfaces to road segments or grid cells ( Gunson et al., 2011 ; Bell et al., 2024 ; Pagany, 2022 ) . These ML applications are crucial when siting a wildlife crossing structures but they do not answer the question: which of these records are wildlife collisions, and how many did we fail to record? A risk map cannot answer either. It assigns a severity score to a place, not a label to a record, and it is typically fitted against synthetic non-collision points rather than against the real crash records in the agency’s database. We address this crucial gap accordingly. Treating each crash record as the unit of analysis turns WVC surveillance into two coupled problems: detecting which records describe animal involvement using only fields that do not encode the answer, and estimating what fraction of records are WVCs when the coded label is itself unreliable. The second problem has an established solution outside transportation. Quantification learning estimates class prevalence in a target sample directly from classifier scores, and does so reliably even when record-level classification is mediocre and the positive class is rare ( Forman, 2008 ; González et al., 2018 ) . Applied to crash data, it converts a classifier into an auditing instrument: the difference between the estimated prevalence and the agency’s own coded rate is a direct measure of under-reporting. Figure 1 places the three questions in sequence. Figure 1: Research Framing: Record-level detection and prevalence estimation. T = True, F=False This paper makes five contributions. First, it establishes that record-level WVC detection is feasible from routinely collected structured fields alone, across four states and 4.9 million crashes, without any field that names an animal. Second, it shows that the ceiling on detection is set by how rich a crash is described rather than by how prevalent WVCs are, and defends that claim with a within-state analysis that holds prevalence fixed while varying record richness. Third, it introduces a reusable label-leakage screen that both prevents circular models and doubles as a reporting-practice audit, revealing that one state encodes animal involvement redundantly across ordinary descriptor fields. Fourth, it decomposes cross-state transfer, showing that record ranking survives transfer while calibration and decision thresholds do not, which bounds what a borrowed model can legitimately be used for. Fifth, it recovers WVC prevalence without labels and converts the result into an under-reporting estimate that agencies can compute on their own files.

sections.heading: 2.1 A Burden Measured by Its Absence
sections.text: The WVC under-reporting literature has circled the same quantity for a decade without estimating it. Snow et al. (2015) approached it as a robustness question, deleting reported deer and moose collisions at increasing rates and watching logistic-regression coefficients and predictive AUC degrade. Their reassuring answer, that inference survives until roughly seventy percent of records are missing, rests on WVCs clustering in low-variance hotspots, and it licenses the continued use of imperfect databases. Jørgensen et al. (2025) complicate that optimism from the opposite side. Where Snow and colleagues simulated random loss, they document a policy-driven loss that pushed North Dakota’s reported counts far below any tolerable threshold, and they show the damage is done not by bias but by sample-size collapse. Read together, the two papers bracket the risk: under-reporting is survivable until a reporting rule changes, at which point it is not. Neither study attempts recovery, and the field’s two strongest empirical anchors stop at the same boundary. Wilkins et al. (2019) quantify the Texas burden in dollars and document the carcass-to-report ratio that defines the missing mass, but model county-level counts by ordinary least squares and take the animal-related label as given. Zou et al. (2019) come closest to the target, coupling a negative-binomial collision-count model to a latent reporting process through a Gaussian copula and showing that ignoring under-reporting biases covariate effects. Their approach is parametric, operates on segment counts rather than records, and requires carcass removals as a second measurement of the same process. Where carcass data do not exist, and in most states they do not, the method has nothing to condition on. Ascensão et al. (2019) widen the frame usefully by arguing that a zero in a mortality record can mean extirpation or a barrier effect rather than low risk, though as a perspective piece it supplies motivation rather than machinery.

sections.heading: 2.2 Machine Learning That Answers “Where”
sections.text: The predictive literature inherited its question from the review that organized it. Gunson et al. (2011) synthesized twenty-four generalized linear models of WVC location, catalogued the predictors that recur, warned that many published effects are confounded, and called for models whose predictive power is demonstrated in landscapes other than the one they were fitted in. Subsequent work answered the call for better estimators more readily than the call for honest transfer testing. Bell et al. (2024) treat Montana’s segment-level carcass counts as an imbalance problem, using SMOTE to rebalance zero-heavy segments before fitting negative binomial and random forest models. The framing is instructive because it is the one our results contradict: rarity is cast as the obstacle, and resampling as the remedy. Pagany (2022) push furthest on generalization, fitting random forests, neural networks, and support vector machines to roughly 731,000 Bavarian police-reported WVCs at hourly and 25-metre resolution, then testing transfer both spatially and forward in time, and reporting success on both. That success deserves qualification. The negative class consists of randomly generated non-accident points, so the model never distinguishes a wildlife crash from an ordinary one; the training class ratio is chosen rather than observed, which sidesteps prevalence entirely; and transfer is tested between regions of a single country under one reporting regime. None of these studies screens for fields that encode the outcome, and none reports calibration.

sections.heading: 2.3 Detecting Records That Were Labelled Wrongly
sections.text: The methodological analog to our task sits outside the WVC literature, in work that treats the crash database itself as the object of correction. Hosseini et al. (2023) apply text mining to police narratives to separate genuine wrong-way driving crashes from records merely flagged as candidates, reaching roughly 82 percent accuracy and cutting the manual review burden on a rare, severe crash type, which is structurally the same problem WVCs present. Bhagat et al. (2025) pursue misclassified intersection-related crashes in Iowa, and report a result that anticipates ours from an independent direction: fusing narrative text with structured fields cut error rates by 54 percent, which is the qualitative form of the completeness effect we quantify. Both approaches depend on free-text narratives, which are frequently unavailable, inconsistently written, and encumbered by privacy restrictions. Neither estimates prevalence, and neither tests transfer across agencies.

sections.heading: 2.4 Counting Without Labels
sections.text: Estimating the proportion of positives in an unlabelled sample is a task in its own right, and one that behaves differently from classification. Forman (2008) proved that naive classify-and-count is biased whenever test prevalence departs from training prevalence, introduced the adjusted estimator that inverts the classifier’s error rates, and demonstrated that prevalence can be recovered reliably even when per-record accuracy is poor and positives are rare, which is precisely the regime crash data occupy. Saerens et al. (2002) arrive at the same destination by a different route, re-estimating the target prior through an expectation-maximization procedure that maximizes the likelihood of the unlabelled sample and returns the new prevalence as a by-product. González et al. (2018) place both within a taxonomy and, importantly for our design, prescribe evaluating quantifiers by systematically varying test prevalence rather than reporting a single number. The failure conditions matter as much as the methods. Esuli et al. (2021) stress-tested the expectation-maximization estimator and found it dependable only when the classification scheme has few classes and the classifier is calibrated, degrading and often failing to converge otherwise. That result anticipates the cross-state behaviour we report.

sections.heading: 2.5 Where This Work Sits
sections.text: Four literatures converge here and have not previously been combined. The under-reporting literature identifies the quantity worth measuring but stops at documentation or requires a second data source. The WVC machine-learning literature builds capable models of the wrong question, against synthetic negatives, without leakage screening or calibration reporting. The crash-record mining literature demonstrates that mislabelled records can be recovered, but only through narratives and only within one agency. Quantification learning supplies the estimator the first literature lacks, together with an explicit account of when it should not be trusted. This paper joins them on structured crash fields that every state already collects.

sections.heading: 3 DATA
sections.text: We assembled complete crash files from four state departments of transportation, chosen to span a wide range of both WVC prevalence and record richness while remaining within a single reporting culture. Table 1 summarizes them. The pooled corpus contains 4,912,128 records with valid coordinates and a non-missing animal label. Each state marks animal involvement in a single binary field, but not with the same meaning. Colorado’s wildlife_related and Utah’s wild_animal_related refer specifically to wild animals, whereas the Iowa and Illinois flags are derived from broader animal-crash coding that does not everywhere separate wild from domestic animals. Wilkins et al. (2019) found domestic animals in 31 percent of Texas animal-related reports, so this distinction is material and we treat it as a bound on cross-state label comparability rather than as noise to be ignored. Since every model is trained and evaluated against the label of its own state, the distinction affects transfer and cross-state prevalence comparisons but not the per-state results. Prevalence varies by nearly a factor of four across the four states, from 3.75 percent in Colorado to 13.96 percent in Iowa. Record richness varies independently: Utah describes a crash with 23 usable fields and Iowa with eight, despite Iowa’s much higher WVC rate. That the two quantities vary independently is what makes the four states a usable design rather than a convenience sample. Roadway attributes were attached by a nearest-segment spatial join in the CONUS Albers equal-area projection (EPSG:5070), matching each crash to the closest attributed centerline segment within 150 m and transferring annual average daily traffic, posted speed, through-lane count, an urban–rural indicator, and a segment sinuosity ratio. Attribute availability differs sharply by state: Utah’s statewide centerline carries traffic attributes only on the state-highway subset, Utah’s through-lane field is effectively empty, and Iowa’s route layer carries no traffic attributes at all and segments too long for sinuosity to mean anything. Roadway variables therefore enter only the harmonized cross-state feature set described below, never the per-state models, and Iowa contributes no roadway attributes. sections.heading: 4 METHOD
sections.text: Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline. The remainder of this section develops each stage. Figure 2: Analysis pipeline.

sections.heading: 4.1 Problem Formulation
sections.text: Let a crash file be a set of records { ( 𝐱 i , y i ) } i = 1 n \{(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} where 𝐱 i \mathbf{x}_{i} represents each structured field a responding officer completed and y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicates animal involvement as coded by the agency. Two quantities are of interest. The first is the posterior Pr ⁡ ( y = 1 ∣ 𝐱 ) \Pr(y=1\mid\mathbf{x}) , which supports record-level detection. The second is the marginal π = Pr ⁡ ( y = 1 ) \pi=\Pr(y=1) , the prevalence, which supports burden estimation. The distinction matters because the two are recovered under different assumptions and, as our transfer results show, survive domain change to different degrees. Crucially, y y is the coded label, not ground truth. Where an agency fails to record animal involvement, y i = 0 y_{i}=0 for a record that is in fact a WVC. We put this asymmetry to work: a model fitted to partially corrupted labels still assigns high scores to unrecorded WVCs, because their covariate signature is unchanged.

sections.heading: 4.2 Label-Leakage Screen
sections.text: Crash schemas contain fields that encode the outcome directly. A first-harmful-event field with the value animal is not a predictor of a WVC; it is the label under another name. Models built on such fields report near-perfect accuracy that reflects nothing but circularity, a failure mode documented across seventeen scientific fields by Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) under the heading of feature leakage. No prior WVC study we are aware of screens for it. We therefore apply an explicit screen before any model is fitted. A candidate field f f , taking value X f X_{f} in 𝒱 f \mathcal{V}_{f} , is excluded when some single value is both overwhelmingly associated with the positive class and accounts for a substantial share of all positives: exclude f ⟺ some value v has Pr ⁡ ( y = 1 ∣ X f = v ) ⏟ purity ≥ τ r and Pr ⁡ ( X f = v ∣ y = 1 ) ⏟ coverage ≥ τ c . \text{exclude }f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{some value }v\text{ has}\quad\underbrace{\Pr(y{=}1\mid X_{f}{=}v)}_{\text{purity}}\geq\tau_{r}\quad\text{and}\quad\underbrace{\Pr(X_{f}{=}v\mid y{=}1)}_{\text{coverage}}\geq\tau_{c}. (1) Purity is the share of records carrying value v v that are WVCs; coverage is the share of all WVCs that carry value v v . A field is excluded when some value scores high on both, with τ r = 0.85 \tau_{r}=0.85 and τ c = 0.15 \tau_{c}=0.15 . These thresholds are discretionary: the appropriate value depends on the schema being screened, and the leakage literature offers no general criterion, only qualitative detection heuristics that require domain knowledge ( Kaufman et al., 2012 ) . Both screen conditions are important. Purity alone would discard a rare value that happens to be wildlife-dominated but explains almost nothing; coverage alone would discard common values with no diagnostic power. The pair isolates fields that function as a restatement of the label while leaving genuinely predictive covariates intact. Single-vehicle involvement, for instance, carries Pr ⁡ ( y = 1 ∣ single vehicle ) ≈ 0.19 \Pr(y=1\mid\text{single vehicle})\approx 0.19 in Colorado and is retained. The screen deliberately runs over a candidate set that includes the suspect fields, so that we can audit its decisions, and its output is reported as a substantive result. Identifiers, names, coordinates, free text, raw timestamps, and outcome counts are excluded beforehand as non-descriptors. Three derived temporal fields (month, hour of day, and day of week) are added for every state; they cannot encode the label and are available universally.

sections.heading: 4.3 Redundancy Screen
sections.text: Leakage and collinearity are separate concerns, so we also screen for redundant predictors before interpreting importances. Variance inflation factors and Pearson correlations assume continuous, roughly linear predictors, whereas these fields are almost all categorical and the few numeric ones are heavily right-skewed. We therefore measure association with a mixed-type, distribution-free matrix: bias-corrected Cramér’s V V for two categorical fields, the correlation ratio for a categorical field against a numeric one, and the absolute Spearman coefficient for two numeric fields, each scaled to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] so a single benchmark applies. Temporal fields count as categorical, and field typing follows the model exactly, so the redundancy we measure is the redundancy the model sees. Any pair reaching 0.80 0.80 is reduced by the greedy correlation-filter rule of Kuhn, 2008 , which drops the field with the highest mean association until no surviving pair clears the benchmark. The adopted cutoff sits between the ecological convention of 0.7 ( Dormann et al., 2013 ) and the caret default of 0.90 ( Kuhn, 2008 ) . Across the four states only two pairs reach the benchmark, both in Illinois and both involving the national-highway-system indicator, which is 0.97 0.97 associated with class of trafficway and 0.95 0.95 with roadway functional class. The rule resolves the resulting three-field cluster by dropping that single indicator. Both decisions rest on Cram’er’s V V , which carries no distributional assumption. The only skew-sensitive measure, the correlation ratio, arises for one field in Colorado with a maximum association of 0.24; recomputing it on log and rank transforms raises that value only to 0.30, well below the benchmark. No merge therefore depends on the distributional form of the data.

sections.heading: 4.4 Classifier and Calibration
sections.text: Crash records are wide, categorical, and non-smooth in the target, which is the regime in which tree ensembles retain a decisive advantage over deep architectures even under heavy tuning ( Grinsztajn et al., 2022 ) . We use CatBoost ( Prokhorenkova et al., 2018 ) , whose ordered target statistics handle the high-cardinality categorical fields natively without the target leakage that ordinary target encoding introduces, an algorithmic counterpart to the data-level screen of Equation 1 . Models use 400–600 boosting iterations at depth 8 and learning rate 0.08, with balanced class weights and a fixed seed. Random forests ( Breiman, 2001 ) and histogram gradient boosting ( Pedregosa et al., 2011 ) are fitted as controls to establish that results reflect the data rather than the estimator. Boosted trees rank well but return distorted probabilities, and ranking quality and calibration quality are decoupled ( Guo et al., 2017 ) . Prevalence estimation consumes posteriors rather than ranks, so calibration is not optional here. We fit an isotonic calibrator on a held-out calibration split, following the demonstration by Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005) that isotonic regression specifically repairs boosted full trees. Training data are split 80/20 into fitting and calibration partitions, stratified jointly by state and label, with the test partition held out entirely. Throughout, we write p i = Pr ⁡ ( y = 1 ∣ 𝐱 i ) p_{i}=\Pr(y{=}1\mid\mathbf{x}_{i}) for the calibrated posterior of record i i , the quantity the estimators below consume.

sections.heading: 4.5 Two Feature Regimes
sections.text: Two questions require two feature spaces, and conflating them would confound the results. For per-state detection, richness analysis, and explanation, each state is modelled on its own leakage-screened fields. This measures what a state can achieve with the record it actually keeps, which is the quantity a data manager cares about, and it is the only regime in which the richness comparison is meaningful. For cross-state transfer and quantification, a common feature space is unavoidable. We harmonize to fourteen variables shared by all four states: eight numeric (single-vehicle indicator, annual average daily traffic, posted speed, lane count, sinuosity, month, hour, day of week) and six categorical (weather, lighting, surface condition, severity, junction type, urban–rural). Each state’s native vocabulary is mapped to a shared code list: weather to clear, rain, snow, fog, or wind; lighting to daylight, dark-lighted, dark-unlighted, or dusk-dawn; severity to property-damage-only, injury, or fatal. Junction type required state-specific derivation to remain non-circular, since Iowa’s obvious junction fields fail the leakage screen; there it is derived from whether the location description names two cross-streets. Numeric fields are median-imputed and categorical fields mode-imputed and one-hot encoded.

sections.heading: 4.6 Evaluation
sections.text: With positives rare and their rate differing across states, average precision is the primary metric. Under class imbalance the receiver operating characteristic is dominated by true negatives and reports optimistically, while the precision–recall baseline equals prevalence and therefore remains informative ( Saito and Rehmsmeier, 2015 ) . Average precision is computed as the prevalence-weighted mean of precision over the recall range, AP = ∑ k ( R k − R k − 1 ) ​ P k , \mathrm{AP}=\sum_{k}\left(R_{k}-R_{k-1}\right)P_{k}, (2) with P k P_{k} and R k R_{k} the precision and recall at the k k th threshold. Average precision approaches π \pi for an uninformative model and equals one for a perfect ranking, so raw values are not comparable across states of differing prevalence. Alongside each value we therefore report a prevalence-neutral skill score that rescales average precision to the interval between chance and perfection, S = AP − π 1 − π , S=\frac{\mathrm{AP}-\pi}{1-\pi}, (3) where S = 0 S=0 corresponds to chance performance and S = 1 S=1 to a perfect ranking. Precision, recall, and F 1 F_{1} are reported at the threshold maximizing F 1 F_{1} on the precision–recall curve. All headline metrics carry 95 percent percentile confidence intervals from 500 test-set bootstrap resamples. Random splits would overstate transferability, since state boundaries coincide with reporting regime, road network, and species assemblage. Following Roberts et al. (2017) , each state is treated as a block and transfer is evaluated leave-one-state-out.

sections.heading: 4.7 Isolating Richness from Rarity
sections.text: A four-state comparison confounds record richness with prevalence, labelling convention, and reporting culture. To separate them we vary richness within each state, holding everything else fixed. Fields are ranked by importance from a full-feature fit, then re-fitted cumulatively, adding one field at a time and recording average precision with 95 percent bootstrap intervals at each step. Training and test partitions are capped at 400,000 and 150,000 records to keep the ∑ s | ℱ s | = 61 \sum_{s}|\mathcal{F}_{s}|=61 fits tractable, where ℱ s \mathcal{F}_{s} is state s s ’s field set. A rising curve within a single state, at a single prevalence, is direct evidence that the recorded field set governs detection. Comparing curve endpoints against a matched field budget then separates the state effect from the richness effect.

sections.heading: 4.9 Under-Reporting Audit
sections.text: Equation 6 reads prevalence from covariate signatures rather than from the animal flag, so its estimate is insensitive to whether the agency coded a given crash correctly. The under-reporting estimate follows directly as Δ ^ = π ^ MLPE − π recorded , \widehat{\Delta}=\hat{\pi}_{\mathrm{MLPE}}-\pi_{\mathrm{recorded}}, (7) the excess of estimated over coded prevalence. Validating Δ ^ \widehat{\Delta} requires a ground truth that no real crash file provides, so we inject one: a known fraction ϕ ∈ { 0 , 0.25 , 0.50 , 0.75 } \phi\in\{0,0.25,0.50,0.75\} of confirmed wildlife crashes is relabelled as non-wildlife, driving the recorded rate to π ⁡ ( 1 − ϕ ) \pi(1-\phi) while the true rate is unchanged, and Δ ^ \widehat{\Delta} is compared against the known gap π ​ ϕ \pi\phi . A complementary experiment tests the record-level counterpart. Rather than correcting an aggregate, we ask whether the individual hidden crashes can be surfaced: the model is retrained on the corrupted labels, and we measure what fraction of the hidden WVCs it still flags at the operating point an agency would have chosen, together with where those crashes sit in the score distribution of records coded non-animal.

sections.heading: 5.1 The Leakage Screen and Iowa’s Under-Coding
sections.text: Equation 1 screens the data before any model is fitted, and it removed the fields that restate the outcome. The resulting pattern is itself informative (Table 2 ). Colorado, Utah, and Illinois each lose only the obvious offenders, a first-harmful-event or crash-type field that is all but synonymous with the animal flag. Iowa loses ten of fifteen. Past the expected harmful-event field, a single sentinel value, 77, recurs across weather, lighting, surface condition, road type, and manner of collision, each roughly 99 percent wildlife and each covering three-quarters of Iowa’s WVCs. That value falls outside the real code range for those fields, so it marks not-applicable: Iowa routes animal crashes through an abbreviated report that leaves the ordinary descriptors blank. The record thins exactly where the crash is a WVC, which leaves Iowa with only eight usable fields and, as the detection results show next, the weakest prevalence-adjusted performance of the four. sections.heading: 5.2 Across States: The Record, Not Prevalence, Sets Detection
sections.text: With the circular fields gone, every state model still separates wildlife crashes from the rest of its file well above chance. Ranking is near-perfect everywhere, with ROC-AUC from 0.967 in Iowa to 0.994 in Utah (Table 3 ). However, average precision better establishes the core argument of this paper. Utah reaches 0.878 and Illinois 0.874, Iowa attains 0.796, and Colorado trails at 0.644 (Figure 3 ). The most informative comparison is Utah against Colorado. The two states carry almost identical WVC prevalence, 4.4 percent and 3.8 percent, so prevalence is held roughly constant between them, yet Utah’s average precision exceeds Colorado’s by a quarter of the scale. The two states differ in the record: Utah describes a crash with 23 screened fields and Colorado with 10. Prevalence cannot account for the difference, whereas richness can. The prevalence-neutral skill score of Equation 3 confirms the same ordering across all four states. The two feature-rich states rank highest and nearly equal, Utah and Illinois at 0.87, feature-poor Colorado ranks lowest at 0.63, and Iowa attains only 0.76 despite carrying the highest prevalence of the four. Detection therefore follows the completeness of the record rather than the rarity of the event, which reverses the emphasis the imbalanced-learning literature places on prevalence as the binding constraint. sections.heading: 5.3 Within a State: Isolating Richness from Prevalence
sections.text: The cross-state comparison entangles richness with everything else that separates one state from another. The within-state curve removes that confound by adding a state’s own fields one at a time, prevalence fixed throughout (Figure 4 ). Detection climbs with every field in all four states. Utah rises from an average precision of 0.16 on its single strongest field to 0.87 on all 23; Colorado climbs the same way but exhausts its record at 10 fields and plateaus at 0.62. Held to a matched eight-field budget, Utah (0.78) and Iowa (0.79) finish level despite Iowa carrying three times Utah’s prevalence, and Colorado lags at 0.58. Same state, same prevalence, more of the record, and detection improves. This is the direct evidence that record completeness, not event prevalence, governs how well WVCs can be found. Figure 4: Within-state richness curves: average precision rises as fields are added, prevalence fixed.

sections.heading: 5.4 What the Models Read
sections.text: Reading Utah, the richest record, with Shapley values shows a coherent physical signature (Figure 5 ). The strongest contributors are roadway departure, manner of collision, hour of day, junction feature, lighting, and vehicle count, and their directions align: single-vehicle, run-off-road crashes on open non-intersection segments, in darkness, away from peak hours, push a record toward wildlife. That is the profile of an animal entering a rural road at night. Aggregating importance by concept across all four states yields a concrete data-collection recommendation. Time of day and season lead (present in all four states, mean importance share 0.26), followed by vehicle count (all four, 0.22), junction type (three states, 0.10), severity (all four, 0.06), and lighting (three states, 0.05). None of these is exotic or expensive to record. Five fields most agencies already capture carry the bulk of the detectable signal, which is what makes the detection result portable to states beyond these four. Figure 5: Utah: global Shapley importance (left) and per-record effect direction (right).

sections.heading: 5.5 What Transfers Across States
sections.text: A model trained on three states and applied to the fourth keeps its ranking almost intact: ROC-AUC on the held-out state stays between 0.964 and 0.974, close to the in-domain values of Table 3 . Decisions are another matter. Setting the held-out threshold from prevalence alone recovers 97 to 98 percent of the oracle F 1 F_{1} for Colorado and Utah and 82 percent for Iowa, then collapses to zero for Illinois. The Illinois failure has a precise explanation: the transferred model’s scores on Illinois are compressed so low that the F 1 F_{1} -optimal threshold is 0.017, while the prevalence rule prescribes 0.41, so the model flags almost nothing. Ranking survives the border; calibration does not. Cross-state, a borrowed model is an instrument for screening and ranking, not for per-record decisions at a transplanted threshold.

sections.heading: 5.6 Prevalence, the Under-Count, and Recovering Hidden Records
sections.text: Read from the scores, prevalence recovers with striking accuracy in-domain, independent of the coded flag (Figure 6 ). Across injected prevalences from 2 to 20 percent, mean absolute error is 0.0006 for maximum-likelihood estimation and 0.0008 for adjusted classify-and-count, against 0.0127 for naive classify-and-count, whose error grows as prevalence drifts from the training rate. Across states the estimators behave exactly as the transfer analysis predicts. Where score distributions align they track truth, estimating Colorado’s 3.8 percent at 3.6 and Utah’s 4.4 percent within a point. Where the shift is severe they fail together, reading Iowa’s 14 percent as 1 to 3 and Illinois’s 5.3 percent as effectively zero, the same Illinois collapse the threshold transfer exposed. Prevalence estimation inherits the ranking that crosses borders and the calibration that does not. Figure 6: Prevalence estimated from scores: in-domain against known prevalence (left) and across states (right). The under-count audit follows from this in-domain accuracy. Injecting a known reporting gap into Colorado drives the recorded rate down while the score-based estimate holds at the true 3.8 percent, since the scores do not depend on whether a crash was coded correctly. The recovered gap matches the injected gap almost exactly: 1.89 percent estimated against 1.91 true with half of WVCs uncoded, and 2.84 against 2.86 with three-quarters uncoded. On its own crash file, an agency can quantify the extent to which it under-reports its wildlife collisions. The audit reaches individual records as well as the aggregate. Corrupting the labels to simulate under-reporting, by hiding a fraction of known wildlife crashes and retraining on the result, fails to hide those crashes from the model. Whatever the fraction concealed, the hidden WVCs land at the 97th to 99th percentile of records coded non-animal, and with half of them hidden the model re-flags 86 percent at the operating point an agency would use. The same model reconstructs descriptors left blank, predicting each held-out field from the others well above its majority baseline: surface condition at 0.92 against 0.82, lighting at 0.84 against 0.70, weather at 0.81 against 0.71, and junction at 0.63 against 0.47. One model detects the collision, surfaces the crashes an agency failed to log, and backfills the fields it left blank.

sections.heading: 6 DISCUSSION
sections.text: The prevailing approach to wildlife crashes in imbalanced data treats their scarcity as the central obstacle and applies resampling to address it. Our results locate the constraint elsewhere. Utah and Colorado detect at nearly the same prevalence, yet Utah’s average precision exceeds Colorado’s by roughly a quarter of the scale because Utah records more than twice as many fields. The within-state curves demonstrate this directly: with a state held fixed and its own fields added one at a time, detection improves at each step. Detection is limited by the completeness of the report, and no synthetic rebalancing recovers information a form never captured. The record itself is therefore where an agency can intervene. This reframing changes what a department can do with records it already holds. A calibrated model trained on screened fields surfaces wildlife crashes an officer never coded as such. With half of Colorado’s WVCs concealed, the hidden crashes still sit at the 98th percentile of records marked non-animal, and the model re-flags most of them at an ordinary operating point. The same model imputes descriptors left blank, recovering surface condition and lighting well above their base rates. Run over a legacy file, it becomes an instrument for retrospective cleanup and quality control. The leakage screen carries its own diagnostic, and applied to Iowa it exposed a coding path that stamps a not-applicable sentinel across five ordinary fields on animal crashes, thinning the record exactly where the crash is a WVC. Any department can apply the same screen to its own data to identify where its reporting practice breaks down. The prevalence machinery turns the classifier into an auditing instrument. In-domain it recovers the true WVC rate to within 0.001 across a tenfold range of prevalence, and it reconstructs an injected reporting gap almost exactly, estimating a 1.9 percent under-count against a 1.9 percent truth. An agency can therefore put a defensible number on how many wildlife collisions its file omits, working from that file alone. That number converts to dollars through established per-collision costs and gives mitigation spending an evidence base, and it needs no carcass-removal survey to produce, which is the second data source the closest prior method requires ( Zou et al., 2019 ) . Cross-state behaviour marks the boundary of the method honestly. Ranking survives a state border almost intact, with held-out ROC-AUC between 0.96 and 0.97, so a borrowed model still separates likely wildlife crashes from the rest. Calibration does not survive, and decisions set at a transplanted threshold can collapse, as they did for Illinois. A model trained elsewhere therefore serves for screening and for prevalence estimation where score distributions align, and it should carry local calibration before it renders per-record verdicts in a new state. The concept importances point to a short, actionable list for reporting manuals. Time of day and season, vehicle count, junction type, severity, and lighting carry most of the detectable signal, and all five are inexpensive and already common. States that record them well make every result here reproducible on their own data. Several assumptions bound these claims. Four states support the richness argument within each of them, though a wider sample would test how far it generalizes. The animal label differs across states, wild-only in Colorado and Utah and broader in Iowa and Illinois, so the per-state results stand on their own footing while cross-state prevalence comparisons carry that caveat. The under-count audit assumes reporting failures fall roughly evenly across the recorded fields. Where an agency omits a distinct slice of crashes, the covariate signature of the missing records shifts, and recovery degrades through the same mechanism that collapses cross-state estimation under severe distribution shift. The under-reporting validation also injects a known gap into a single state, so it demonstrates the mechanism rather than a field-measured rate. Confirming the audit against independent carcass counts is the natural next step.

sections.heading: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.text: We recast wildlife-vehicle collision surveillance from a spatial question, where collisions concentrate, to a record question, which crashes are collisions and how many go uncounted. Across 4.9 million crashes in four states, calibrated gradient-boosted models detect wildlife crashes from ordinary fields alone, and the completeness of the record, not the rarity of the event, sets how well they detect. Read as scores in place of labels, the same models estimate a state’s true WVC prevalence and measure the gap between that estimate and the rate the agency recorded. The returns for practice are immediate: surfacing collisions never logged, backfilling missing fields, quantifying a true collision burden for mitigation funding, and naming the handful of fields a reporting manual should require. Extending the framework across more states, and validating the under-count against independent carcass data, would carry a demonstrated instrument into standard transportation practice.

Mkufya Recovering Hidden Wildlife–Vehicle Collisions from Existing Crash Data: A Cross-State Framework for Detection, Prevalence Estimation, and Under-Reporting Audits Rasheed Bello* South Carolina State University Orangeburg SC 29117 USA ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0007-7918-1703 Email: rbello@scsu.edu Judith Mwakalonge South Carolina State University Orangeburg SC 29117 USA Email: jmwakalo@scsu.edu Varghese Vaidyan Dakota State University Madison SD 57042 USA Email:varghese.vaidyan@dsu.edu Vijay Bendigeri Independent Researcher Sacramento CA USA Email: vijaybendigeri@gmail.com Anthony Dontoh South Carolina State University Orangeburg SC 29117 USA Email: adontoh@scsu.edu Gurcan Comert North Carolina A&T State University Greensboro NC 27411 USA Email: gcomert@ncat.edu Miriam Mkufya South Carolina State University Orangeburg SC 29117 USA Email: mmkufya@scsu.edu Abstract Objectives Wildlife–vehicle collisions (WVCs) impose a large and poorly measured toll on United States highways, yet most state crash databases never record which crashes involved an animal, so agencies cannot say how many they miss. This paper asks whether the crash records agencies already hold can be used to identify WVCs at the record level and to estimate how many go uncoded. Methods We assembled 4.9 million crash records from Colorado, Utah, Iowa, and Illinois, spanning 2007 to 2026. Each state’s schema was passed through a label-leakage screen that removes any field encoding animal involvement, and separately harmonized to a shared vocabulary for cross-state analysis. Labeled wildlife vehicle crashes are treated as ground-truth, with which Calibrated gradient-boosted classifiers were trained per state and read with Shapley additive explanations. Prevalence was then estimated directly from classifier scores using Adjusted Classify-and-Count and Maximum-Likelihood Prevalence Estimation, validated in-domain, across states, and against injected reporting gaps. Findings Detection quality is governed by how completely a crash is recorded, not by how rare WVCs are: at equivalent prevalence near four percent, feature-rich Utah reaches an average precision of 0.88 against 0.64 for feature-poor Colorado, and Utah exceeds Iowa despite Iowa’s threefold higher prevalence. A within-state richness curve with bootstrap confidence intervals confirms the effect with prevalence held fixed. Models rank records almost perfectly everywhere, but their calibration does not transfer, and prevalence estimates recover the true rate to within 0.001 in-domain. Novelty This work reframes WVC surveillance from predicting where collisions cluster to detecting which records are collisions and estimating how many are missing, using only data agencies already collect. Practical Applications Agencies can retrospectively flag unlogged WVCs in legacy files, quantify their true collision burden for mitigation funding, and learn which crash-report fields most improve detection before revising a reporting manual. Keywords : wildlife–vehicle collisions, crash records, under-reporting, quantification learning, gradient boosting, data quality 1 INTRODUCTION Collisions between vehicles and large wild animals are among the most common crash types on rural highways yet among the least visible in the data that transportation agencies use to set priorities ( Bell et al., 2024 ; Jørgensen et al., 2025 ) . Wildlife-Vehicle Crashes (WVC) cost the United States above eight billion dollars, alongside tens of thousands of injuries and close to two hundred deaths ( Bell et al., 2024 ) . Earlier national accounting put large-mammal collisions at one to two million per year ( Huijser et al., 2009 ) . Texas alone recorded 51,522 animal-related crashes between 2010 and 2016, costing motorists roughly $1.3 billion annually ( Wilkins et al., 2019 ) . These figures share a fundamental limitation. Every one of them is built from crashes that were reported, coded, and retained, and the literature is unanimous that this is a fraction of what occurs. Maintenance crews recover five to ten carcasses for every collision that reaches a police report ( Wilkins et al., 2019 ) , and Montana’s transportation department counted 60,858 carcasses over a decade against 23,718 collisions logged by highway patrol over the same period ( Bell et al., 2024 ) . Despite the significant disparities, there has been no unified method to estimate the cost of unreported WVCs. This needed capability to address this gap is hinged on state crash reporting rules, which establishes what is recorded into crash report, and how. When North Dakota narrowed its reporting requirement to injury and fatality crashes in 2013, annual reported WVCs fell from 3,488 to 133, and seasonal effects that had been statistically detectable before the change became invisible afterwards purely through loss of sample size ( Jørgensen et al., 2025 ) . The same administrative dynamics that decides whether a crash is recorded also decides how richly it is described, and both decisions propagate into every downstream analysis an agency performs. Machine learning (ML) has been applied to this problem from a different perspective. A decade of work has treated WVCs as a spatial phenomenon and asked where collisions concentrate, fitting risk surfaces to road segments or grid cells ( Gunson et al., 2011 ; Bell et al., 2024 ; Pagany, 2022 ) . These ML applications are crucial when siting a wildlife crossing structures but they do not answer the question: which of these records are wildlife collisions, and how many did we fail to record? A risk map cannot answer either. It assigns a severity score to a place, not a label to a record, and it is typically fitted against synthetic non-collision points rather than against the real crash records in the agency’s database. We address this crucial gap accordingly. Treating each crash record as the unit of analysis turns WVC surveillance into two coupled problems: detecting which records describe animal involvement using only fields that do not encode the answer, and estimating what fraction of records are WVCs when the coded label is itself unreliable. The second problem has an established solution outside transportation. Quantification learning estimates class prevalence in a target sample directly from classifier scores, and does so reliably even when record-level classification is mediocre and the positive class is rare ( Forman, 2008 ; González et al., 2018 ) . Applied to crash data, it converts a classifier into an auditing instrument: the difference between the estimated prevalence and the agency’s own coded rate is a direct measure of under-reporting. Figure 1 places the three questions in sequence. Figure 1: Research Framing: Record-level detection and prevalence estimation. T = True, F=False This paper makes five contributions. First, it establishes that record-level WVC detection is feasible from routinely collected structured fields alone, across four states and 4.9 million crashes, without any field that names an animal. Second, it shows that the ceiling on detection is set by how rich a crash is described rather than by how prevalent WVCs are, and defends that claim with a within-state analysis that holds prevalence fixed while varying record richness. Third, it introduces a reusable label-leakage screen that both prevents circular models and doubles as a reporting-practice audit, revealing that one state encodes animal involvement redundantly across ordinary descriptor fields. Fourth, it decomposes cross-state transfer, showing that record ranking survives transfer while calibration and decision thresholds do not, which bounds what a borrowed model can legitimately be used for. Fifth, it recovers WVC prevalence without labels and converts the result into an under-reporting estimate that agencies can compute on their own files. 2 RELATED WORK 2.1 A Burden Measured by Its Absence The WVC under-reporting literature has circled the same quantity for a decade without estimating it. Snow et al. (2015) approached it as a robustness question, deleting reported deer and moose collisions at increasing rates and watching logistic-regression coefficients and predictive AUC degrade. Their reassuring answer, that inference survives until roughly seventy percent of records are missing, rests on WVCs clustering in low-variance hotspots, and it licenses the continued use of imperfect databases. Jørgensen et al. (2025) complicate that optimism from the opposite side. Where Snow and colleagues simulated random loss, they document a policy-driven loss that pushed North Dakota’s reported counts far below any tolerable threshold, and they show the damage is done not by bias but by sample-size collapse. Read together, the two papers bracket the risk: under-reporting is survivable until a reporting rule changes, at which point it is not. Neither study attempts recovery, and the field’s two strongest empirical anchors stop at the same boundary. Wilkins et al. (2019) quantify the Texas burden in dollars and document the carcass-to-report ratio that defines the missing mass, but model county-level counts by ordinary least squares and take the animal-related label as given. Zou et al. (2019) come closest to the target, coupling a negative-binomial collision-count model to a latent reporting process through a Gaussian copula and showing that ignoring under-reporting biases covariate effects. Their approach is parametric, operates on segment counts rather than records, and requires carcass removals as a second measurement of the same process. Where carcass data do not exist, and in most states they do not, the method has nothing to condition on. Ascensão et al. (2019) widen the frame usefully by arguing that a zero in a mortality record can mean extirpation or a barrier effect rather than low risk, though as a perspective piece it supplies motivation rather than machinery. 2.2 Machine Learning That Answers “Where” The predictive literature inherited its question from the review that organized it. Gunson et al. (2011) synthesized twenty-four generalized linear models of WVC location, catalogued the predictors that recur, warned that many published effects are confounded, and called for models whose predictive power is demonstrated in landscapes other than the one they were fitted in. Subsequent work answered the call for better estimators more readily than the call for honest transfer testing. Bell et al. (2024) treat Montana’s segment-level carcass counts as an imbalance problem, using SMOTE to rebalance zero-heavy segments before fitting negative binomial and random forest models. The framing is instructive because it is the one our results contradict: rarity is cast as the obstacle, and resampling as the remedy. Pagany (2022) push furthest on generalization, fitting random forests, neural networks, and support vector machines to roughly 731,000 Bavarian police-reported WVCs at hourly and 25-metre resolution, then testing transfer both spatially and forward in time, and reporting success on both. That success deserves qualification. The negative class consists of randomly generated non-accident points, so the model never distinguishes a wildlife crash from an ordinary one; the training class ratio is chosen rather than observed, which sidesteps prevalence entirely; and transfer is tested between regions of a single country under one reporting regime. None of these studies screens for fields that encode the outcome, and none reports calibration. 2.3 Detecting Records That Were Labelled Wrongly The methodological analog to our task sits outside the WVC literature, in work that treats the crash database itself as the object of correction. Hosseini et al. (2023) apply text mining to police narratives to separate genuine wrong-way driving crashes from records merely flagged as candidates, reaching roughly 82 percent accuracy and cutting the manual review burden on a rare, severe crash type, which is structurally the same problem WVCs present. Bhagat et al. (2025) pursue misclassified intersection-related crashes in Iowa, and report a result that anticipates ours from an independent direction: fusing narrative text with structured fields cut error rates by 54 percent, which is the qualitative form of the completeness effect we quantify. Both approaches depend on free-text narratives, which are frequently unavailable, inconsistently written, and encumbered by privacy restrictions. Neither estimates prevalence, and neither tests transfer across agencies. 2.4 Counting Without Labels Estimating the proportion of positives in an unlabelled sample is a task in its own right, and one that behaves differently from classification. Forman (2008) proved that naive classify-and-count is biased whenever test prevalence departs from training prevalence, introduced the adjusted estimator that inverts the classifier’s error rates, and demonstrated that prevalence can be recovered reliably even when per-record accuracy is poor and positives are rare, which is precisely the regime crash data occupy. Saerens et al. (2002) arrive at the same destination by a different route, re-estimating the target prior through an expectation-maximization procedure that maximizes the likelihood of the unlabelled sample and returns the new prevalence as a by-product. González et al. (2018) place both within a taxonomy and, importantly for our design, prescribe evaluating quantifiers by systematically varying test prevalence rather than reporting a single number. The failure conditions matter as much as the methods. Esuli et al. (2021) stress-tested the expectation-maximization estimator and found it dependable only when the classification scheme has few classes and the classifier is calibrated, degrading and often failing to converge otherwise. That result anticipates the cross-state behaviour we report. 2.5 Where This Work Sits Four literatures converge here and have not previously been combined. The under-reporting literature identifies the quantity worth measuring but stops at documentation or requires a second data source. The WVC machine-learning literature builds capable models of the wrong question, against synthetic negatives, without leakage screening or calibration reporting. The crash-record mining literature demonstrates that mislabelled records can be recovered, but only through narratives and only within one agency. Quantification learning supplies the estimator the first literature lacks, together with an explicit account of when it should not be trusted. This paper joins them on structured crash fields that every state already collects. 3 DATA We assembled complete crash files from four state departments of transportation, chosen to span a wide range of both WVC prevalence and record richness while remaining within a single reporting culture. Table 1 summarizes them. The pooled corpus contains 4,912,128 records with valid coordinates and a non-missing animal label. Each state marks animal involvement in a single binary field, but not with the same meaning. Colorado’s wildlife_related and Utah’s wild_animal_related refer specifically to wild animals, whereas the Iowa and Illinois flags are derived from broader animal-crash coding that does not everywhere separate wild from domestic animals. Wilkins et al. (2019) found domestic animals in 31 percent of Texas animal-related reports, so this distinction is material and we treat it as a bound on cross-state label comparability rather than as noise to be ignored. Since every model is trained and evaluated against the label of its own state, the distinction affects transfer and cross-state prevalence comparisons but not the per-state results. Prevalence varies by nearly a factor of four across the four states, from 3.75 percent in Colorado to 13.96 percent in Iowa. Record richness varies independently: Utah describes a crash with 23 usable fields and Iowa with eight, despite Iowa’s much higher WVC rate. That the two quantities vary independently is what makes the four states a usable design rather than a convenience sample. Roadway attributes were attached by a nearest-segment spatial join in the CONUS Albers equal-area projection (EPSG:5070), matching each crash to the closest attributed centerline segment within 150 m and transferring annual average daily traffic, posted speed, through-lane count, an urban–rural indicator, and a segment sinuosity ratio. Attribute availability differs sharply by state: Utah’s statewide centerline carries traffic attributes only on the state-highway subset, Utah’s through-lane field is effectively empty, and Iowa’s route layer carries no traffic attributes at all and segments too long for sinuosity to mean anything. Roadway variables therefore enter only the harmonized cross-state feature set described below, never the per-state models, and Iowa contributes no roadway attributes. We put this asymmetry to work: a model fitted to partially corrupted labels still assigns high scores to unrecorded WVCs, because their covariate signature is unchanged. 4.2 Label-Leakage Screen Crash schemas contain fields that encode the outcome directly. A first-harmful-event field with the value animal is not a predictor of a WVC; it is the label under another name. Models built on such fields report near-perfect accuracy that reflects nothing but circularity, a failure mode documented across seventeen scientific fields by Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) under the heading of feature leakage. No prior WVC study we are aware of screens for it. We therefore apply an explicit screen before any model is fitted. A candidate field f f , taking value X f X_{f} in 𝒱 f \mathcal{V}_{f} , is excluded when some single value is both overwhelmingly associated with the positive class and accounts for a substantial share of all positives: exclude f ⟺ some value v has Pr ⁡ ( y = 1 ∣ X f = v ) ⏟ purity ≥ τ r and Pr ⁡ ( X f = v ∣ y = 1 ) ⏟ coverage ≥ τ c . \text{exclude }f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{some value }v\text{ has}\quad\underbrace{\Pr(y{=}1\mid X_{f}{=}v)}_{\text{purity}}\geq\tau_{r}\quad\text{and}\quad\underbrace{\Pr(X_{f}{=}v\mid y{=}1)}_{\text{coverage}}\geq\tau_{c}. (1) Purity is the share of records carrying value v v that are WVCs; coverage is the share of all WVCs that carry value v v . A field is excluded when some value scores high on both, with τ r = 0.85 \tau_{r}=0.85 and τ c = 0.15 \tau_{c}=0.15 . These thresholds are discretionary: the appropriate value depends on the schema being screened, and the leakage literature offers no general criterion, only qualitative detection heuristics that require domain knowledge ( Kaufman et al., 2012 ) . Both screen conditions are important. Purity alone would discard a rare value that happens to be wildlife-dominated but explains almost nothing; coverage alone would discard common values with no diagnostic power. The pair isolates fields that function as a restatement of the label while leaving genuinely predictive covariates intact. Single-vehicle involvement, for instance, carries Pr ⁡ ( y = 1 ∣ single vehicle ) ≈ 0.19 \Pr(y=1\mid\text{single vehicle})\approx 0.19 in Colorado and is retained. The screen deliberately runs over a candidate set that includes the suspect fields, so that we can audit its decisions, and its output is reported as a substantive result. Identifiers, names, coordinates, free text, raw timestamps, and outcome counts are excluded beforehand as non-descriptors. Three derived temporal fields (month, hour of day, and day of week) are added for every state; they cannot encode the label and are available universally. 4.3 Redundancy Screen Leakage and collinearity are separate concerns, so we also screen for redundant predictors before interpreting importances. Variance inflation factors and Pearson correlations assume continuous, roughly linear predictors, whereas these fields are almost all categorical and the few numeric ones are heavily right-skewed. We therefore measure association with a mixed-type, distribution-free matrix: bias-corrected Cramér’s V V for two categorical fields, the correlation ratio for a categorical field against a numeric one, and the absolute Spearman coefficient for two numeric fields, each scaled to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] so a single benchmark applies. Temporal fields count as categorical, and field typing follows the model exactly, so the redundancy we measure is the redundancy the model sees. Any pair reaching 0.80 0.80 is reduced by the greedy correlation-filter rule of Kuhn, 2008 , which drops the field with the highest mean association until no surviving pair clears the benchmark. The adopted cutoff sits between the ecological convention of 0.7 ( Dormann et al., 2013 ) and the caret default of 0.90 ( Kuhn, 2008 ) . Across the four states only two pairs reach the benchmark, both in Illinois and both involving the national-highway-system indicator, which is 0.97 0.97 associated with class of trafficway and 0.95 0.95 with roadway functional class. The rule resolves the resulting three-field cluster by dropping that single indicator. Both decisions rest on Cram’er’s V V , which carries no distributional assumption. The only skew-sensitive measure, the correlation ratio, arises for one field in Colorado with a maximum association of 0.24; recomputing it on log and rank transforms raises that value only to 0.30, well below the benchmark. No merge therefore depends on the distributional form of the data. 4.4 Classifier and Calibration Crash records are wide, categorical, and non-smooth in the target, which is the regime in which tree ensembles retain a decisive advantage over deep architectures even under heavy tuning ( Grinsztajn et al., 2022 ) . We use CatBoost ( Prokhorenkova et al., 2018 ) , whose ordered target statistics handle the high-cardinality categorical fields natively without the target leakage that ordinary target encoding introduces, an algorithmic counterpart to the data-level screen of Equation 1 . Models use 400–600 boosting iterations at depth 8 and learning rate 0.08, with balanced class weights and a fixed seed. Random forests ( Breiman, 2001 ) and histogram gradient boosting ( Pedregosa et al., 2011 ) are fitted as controls to establish that results reflect the data rather than the estimator. Boosted trees rank well but return distorted probabilities, and ranking quality and calibration quality are decoupled ( Guo et al., 2017 ) . Prevalence estimation consumes posteriors rather than ranks, so calibration is not optional here. We fit an isotonic calibrator on a held-out calibration split, following the demonstration by Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005) that isotonic regression specifically repairs boosted full trees. Training data are split 80/20 into fitting and calibration partitions, stratified jointly by state and label, with the test partition held out entirely. Throughout, we write p i = Pr ⁡ ( y = 1 ∣ 𝐱 i ) p_{i}=\Pr(y{=}1\mid\mathbf{x}_{i}) for the calibrated posterior of record i i , the quantity the estimators below consume. 4.5 Two Feature Regimes Two questions require two feature spaces, and conflating them would confound the results. For per-state detection, richness analysis, and explanation, each state is modelled on its own leakage-screened fields. This measures what a state can achieve with the record it actually keeps, which is the quantity a data manager cares about, and it is the only regime in which the richness comparison is meaningful. For cross-state transfer and quantification, a common feature space is unavoidable. We harmonize to fourteen variables shared by all four states: eight numeric (single-vehicle indicator, annual average daily traffic, posted speed, lane count, sinuosity, month, hour, day of week) and six categorical (weather, lighting, surface condition, severity, junction type, urban–rural). Each state’s native vocabulary is mapped to a shared code list: weather to clear, rain, snow, fog, or wind; lighting to daylight, dark-lighted, dark-unlighted, or dusk-dawn; severity to property-damage-only, injury, or fatal. Junction type required state-specific derivation to remain non-circular, since Iowa’s obvious junction fields fail the leakage screen; there it is derived from whether the location description names two cross-streets. Numeric fields are median-imputed and categorical fields mode-imputed and one-hot encoded. 4.6 Evaluation With positives rare and their rate differing across states, average precision is the primary metric.
